newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai auto makers struggle amid slumping sales.
newsitem.headline: Thai auto makers struggle amid slumping sales.

text.p: Thailand's automobile industry has enjoyed double-digit growth for a decade but is facing a critical test in the severe downturn of the local economy, industry analysts said.
Car sales have slumped as consumer spending slows in line with the flagging economy and cash-strapped finance firms are refusing to give out as many hire-purchase loans as in the past, they said.
"In the memory of the Thai automotive industry, right now is the most difficult time," Tim Dunne, researcher at Bangkok-based research house Automotive Resources Asia Ltd, told Reuters.
"Sales have been growing every year since 1991 at an average of 14 percent per annum, but now (it's) negative growth," he said.

According to data from Toyota Motors (Thailand), total commercial and passenger vehicle sales in the first four months of this year fell 12 percent to 169,721 units from 192,356 in the same period last year.
The slowing car sales since the beginning of this year has prompted most major auto assemblers to cut production and tighten their belts to control costs, analysts said.

"Most car plants have decreased their production capacity by reducing overtime work and not extending contracts for temporary workers," said Surapong Phasitpatnapong, a spokesman for the Thai Automotive Industry Association (TAIA).
Siam Nissan Automobile Co, an assembler and distributor of Nissan brand vehicles in Thailand, said early this month it had laid off 200 temporary workers due to poor automobile demand.
The firm is a joint venture owned 75 percent by Siam Motor and 25 percent by Japan's Nissan Motor Co Ltd.
Surapong said the flagging car sales since the beginning of this year prompted the association to revise down its target of car sales for the whole year to 570,000 units from 600,000 previously.
In 1996, total car sales in Thailand rose 3.1 percent to 589,123 units from 571,580 in the previous year, according to Toyota's statistics.
"The car market is really bad, especially the top market. Luxury car sales have fallen by an average of 30-40 percent this year," said an auto analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govette Asia.
The sales of Mercedes Benz, the most popular luxury car brand in Thailand, dropped by 35 percent to 2,164 units in the first four months from 3,321 in the same period last year, Toyota said.
Tightening of hire purchase loans by most finance companies facing liquidity problems would continue to affect car sales, more than 60 percent of which are financed by borrowings, analysts said.
Most auto makers now turned their attention to the export market to relieve overproduction, they added.
"The foreign market will provide some relief for the auto makers for exporting (their excess supply)," Dunne said.
The export value of assembled vehicles and parts rocketed in the first four months to 6.48 billion baht ($250 million) from 2.93 billion baht in the same period last year.
"The exports of assembled cars and parts will be relatively high this year. The capacity expansion of some auto makers is scheduled to be completed later this year," Surapong said.
